The piece

Built like a wall, detailed like a Victorian pub

A bar has to survive a party. This one is framed like a stud wall — 60 × 40 pine uprights every 400 mm — then given a proper panelled front and capped with a 50 mm solid top that runs the full 3.50 m in one unbroken piece.

The front is the whole difference. Four fluted pilasters stand on the bay lines, and between them sit six panels — 475, 500 and 475 mm wide, 750 tall — each framed by a moulding run round its edge. Those proportions are not arbitrary: a panel taller than it is wide is what makes a bar front read as a pub rather than a kitchen island. Under the top edge, a second moulding brings the apparent thickness to 90 mm, the heavy Victorian line, while the top itself stays the 50 mm slab.

Pine arrives in Jordan in 4.25 m lengths, so that top needs no join anywhere along it. It is glued up from boards, planed flat, then stained down to the dark mahogany tone the look depends on. Three coats of hardwax oil go on it — the same finish used on kitchen worktops. Spills wipe off. In ten years a scratch is sanded back and re-oiled in an afternoon, which is something a lacquered top can never do.

The top overhangs the panelled face by 300 mm. That is not styling, it is knee room. Without it a stool cannot pull in and nobody sits at the bar past the first drink.

Behind it: a 700 mm working aisle, then a back counter at 900 mm — deliberately lower than the bar, so whoever is pouring is not reaching up. The sink bay and the fridge bay are left open in the carcass and cut to whichever appliances you choose. Standing on that counter is the gantry: three arched openings with mirror behind them, shelves for the bottles, a brass rack of glasses hanging under the top shelf, and a cornice at 2.25 m.

Its four posts land at 0, 1150, 2600 and 3450 — every one of them directly over a divider in the counter below. An evenly spaced post would have come down in the middle of the 900 mm sink bay, on nothing. The gantry is also through-bolted back to the wall, so the wall takes the tipping and the counter only carries weight.

The arches are cut in the timber. The mirror behind each one is ordinary rectangular glass, 980 × 620 — shaped glass costs several times as much, arrives slowly and breaks.

The bar runs the full width of the space and dies straight into the wall on the left, so there is one way in and out of the service side — the right-hand end. Nothing gets walked through behind the bar, and the left end needs no finished panel because no one ever sees it.

A brass rail runs the whole length of the bar, 200 mm off the floor. Feet need somewhere to go, and brass is the one the light finds.

Deliverables

Exactly what you receive

  1. Bar unit — 3500 × 700 × 1100 mm. Pine stud carcass; panelled guest face with four fluted pilasters and six moulded panels; 50 mm solid top in one piece with a 300 mm overhang and an applied moulding bringing the edge to 90 mm; three open bays with two fixed shelves each; one panelled end (right); brass foot rail. Runs into the left wall; service side entered from the right end only.
  2. Back counter — 3450 × 400 × 900 mm. 40 mm dark-stained top, five bays: open fridge bay, open sink bay, four soft-close doors, three internal shelves.
  3. Gantry — 3450 × 260 × 1350 mm standing on the back counter, 2250 mm overall. Four fluted posts on the counter dividers, continuous sole plate, three arched openings with mirrors, two shelves, brass stemware rack, moulded cornice. Through-bolted to the wall. Replaces the wall shelf unit.
  4. Finishing — dark mahogany stain throughout, hardwax oil satin, three coats on the bar top.
  5. Delivery and fitting in Amman — scribed to the floor, levelled and fixed.

Not included: sink and tap · under-counter fridge · pendant lights · electrical and plumbing connection · bar stools — optional, quoted separately (see the three directions below). Mirror glass for the gantry is included.

Detail

Five things that decide whether it works

The top

3500 × 700 × 50 mm

Solid pine glue-up, one piece end to end. Eased edge, wire-brushed, three coats of hardwax oil. 300 mm overhang on the stool side.

The panelled face

6 panels · 4 pilasters

Panels of 475, 500 and 475 mm, all 750 tall, each with a moulding run round it. Between them, fluted pilasters with a moulded cap and base. Upright proportions are what separate a pub front from a kitchen island.

The gantry

3450 × 260 × 1350 mm

Three arched openings with mirrors behind, two shelves, a brass rack of stemware, a cornice at 2.25 m. Its posts sit over the counter dividers and it is bolted back to the wall.

The foot rail

Ø42 mm × 3500 mm

Solid brass on four flanges, 200 mm off the floor. Takes the scuffing that would otherwise land on the panels, and it is the thing that catches the lamplight.

The back counter

3450 × 400 × 900 mm

40 mm top in dark stain. Four soft-close doors with black pulls, an open fridge bay and an open sink bay cut to your appliances.

The top edge

50 mm slab · 90 mm edge

The slab stays 50 mm. A cove-and-bullnose moulding applied underneath brings the visible edge to 90 mm — the heavy Victorian line — with its underside at 1010 mm, still clear of seated knees.

The finish

Hardwax oil, satin

Repairable, food-safe once cured, and it keeps the timber feeling like timber. Shown here in three pub stains — use the buttons above the model.

Optional

Five stools, three directions

Stools are a separate piece and nothing here is locked in. These are three directions to give you a feel for how the bar reads with each — switch between them on the model above. Once you know which way you want to go, we cost them with the rest.

A

Solid pine

The same pine as the bar. Square splayed legs, double stretchers, a 360 mm seat at 750 mm, hardwax oil to match.

B

Pine seat, brass-and-black base

A round 370 mm pine seat, 45 mm thick, on a black steel disc base with a foot ring — the bar's timber and the foot rail's steel in one object.

C

Tan leather, black base

A padded tan leather seat on a black base with a foot ring, as in the reference photo. The softest of the three against all that timber.
